world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached
earlier_scan.source_named: Martin, Marieke (2012) A grammar of Wawa, an endangered language of Cameroon. PhD thesis, University of Kent.
earlier_scan.note: Full PhD grammar exists but not retrievable (KAR search reachable, item not exposed; EThOS retired). Glottolog page lists only Blench 2009 classification note.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2009 (draft). The Bantoid languages: a monograph. 51 pp. ms., rogerblench.info (the Internet Archive).
sources.note: Wawa appears only in the Mambiloid tree, map, table of moribund languages and one lexical comparison ('sim' to fly); no prosody.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. Wawa dialects / Wawa: Oumyari dialect. Web pages, Kay Williamson Educational Foundation site (rogerblench.info, Internet Archive copy).
sources.note: States Wawa has four dialects (Oumyari, Ndi, Mbengezhe, Gandu); links only to ethnoscience wordlists (birds, mammals, trees); 'Grammar' heading empty.

sources.citation: Ngaouri, Landri. 2024. Classification linguistique du wawa : langue en danger d'extinction, au Cameroun. Glottopol 40. doi:10.4000/glottopol.4417 (CORE PDF; embedded font garbled, decoded by character shift)
sources.note: Lexical dialectometry Wawa vs Vute/Kwanja; explicitly says tonal opposition was not taken into account in the comparison; lists three Wawa dialects (tikambi, gandwa, jujunbe); no stress or tone description.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce, Sascha Griffiths, Marieke Martin, Laura Hayward & David Zeitlyn. 2021. Language ecology, language endangerment, and relict languages: Case studies from Adamawa (Cameroon-Nigeria). Open Linguistics 7: 244–300. doi:10.1515/opli-2021-0011
sources.note: Sociolinguistic; §6.4 'Linguistic overview' (p. 279–280) says Wawa is among the most morphologically complex Mambiloid languages and that Fulfulde spoken by Wawa shows 'the introduction of tonal contrasts (Martin 2012)'; no statement on stress or on the Wawa tone system itself.

sources.citation: Martin, Marieke. 2009. Documenting Wawa – a Mambiloid language in the Cameroon-Nigeria borderland. Report, Gesellschaft für bedrohte Sprachen (Köln), www.uni-koeln.de/gbs/Berichte/Wawa/ (the Internet Archive 2016 capture).
sources.note: Language-ecology/endangerment report; no phonology; the only 'stress' hits are the English verb.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. n.d. Field trip 1998-9: Mambiloid. 2 pp. notes, rogerblench.info (the Internet Archive).
sources.note: Field notes on survey; nothing on Wawa prosody.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 1993. An outline classification of the Mambiloid languages. Journal of West African Languages 23(1): 105–118. (image scan from rogerblench.info via the Internet Archive; scanned at 300 dpi)
sources.note: §2.2 'Tone' (p. 111): 'Although no overall statement about tone in Mambiloid is yet possible, the group is exceptional for the complexity of its tonal systems and the prevalence of phonemic contour tones' (Vute 3 levels + 8 glides, Kwanja 3 levels, Mambila 4 levels). Wawa treated as the most divergent dialect of Vute (after Guarisma 1987). Nothing on stress; nothing Wawa-specific on prosody.

sources.citation: PHOIBLE 2.0, inventory GM 1647 'Wawa' (contributors Christopher Green & Steven Moran), source: Martin 2012, A grammar of Wawa (PhD, Kent).
sources.note: Segment inventory only (49 segments) including three tone segments: high (˦), mid (˧), low (˨) — i.e. Martin 2012 as coded by PHOIBLE treats Wawa as a three-level tone language; nothing about stress.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2001. An introduction to the Mambiloid languages. In Mutaka & Chumbow (eds.), Research mate in African linguistics: Focus on Cameroon, 79–92. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.

sources.note: Family-level overview by the main Mambiloid phonetician; likely characterises Mambiloid prosody (tone, absence of stress) generally, usable as a second-hand/family statement if Martin 2012 stays unreachable.

sources.note: The only full description of Wawa; PHOIBLE's inventory (with H/M/L tones) is coded from its phonology chapter, which is where any statement on stress/accent vs. tone would be. Not in KAR/CORE/EThOS; needs ILL from Kent (Templeman Library) or a copy from the author.

sources.note: Blench 1993 (after Guarisma 1987) treats Wawa as the most divergent Vute dialect; Guarisma's Vute phonology (3 level + 8 contour tones) is the nearest published prosodic description in the Vute-Wawa cluster, relevant only as a proxy and for the identity question.
